Tutorial 3: Finding and validating hits

Emanuel Michele Soda

Istituto Europeo Oncologia (IEO), Milano, Italy
emanuelsoda@gmail.com

Elena Ceccacci

Istituto Europeo Oncologia (IEO), Milano, Italy
elena.ceccacci@ieo.it

2026-10-25

Source: vignettes/Tutorial_3_Finding_hits.Rmd
Tutorial_3_Finding_hits.Rmd

About this tutorial

A hit is a gene whose barcodes change consistently in the treated samples compared with the control samples. In a dropout (loss of function) screen the interesting hits are usually depleted: their knockdown kills the cells only in the presence of the treatment.

This tutorial goes through the functions of ScreenR that find hits and check them, one step at a time:

  1. tell ScreenR which samples to compare (design matrix and contrasts);
  2. test each gene with FRY, ROAST and CAMERA;
  3. test each gene with the Z-score methods;
  4. compare the methods and combine their results;
  5. use several time points;
  6. check the candidates in the data, barcode by barcode.

It uses the example screen of ScreenR. The complete analysis of this screen, from the quality control to the list of the genes to validate, is in the longitudinal screen vignette; here the focus is on how each function works and how to read its result.

The data 

library(ScreenR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

The plots of ScreenR have no theme of their own: choose one for the whole session with theme_set().

theme_set(theme_light(base_size = 12))

The screen has two samples taken before the treatment (Time1, before the infection, and Time2, after the puromycin selection), then three treated (TRT) and three control (CTRL) replicates 7 days (Time3) and 14 days (Time4) after the selection. The sample_table describes the samples, the groups (used by the statistical models) are the combinations of time point and treatment, and the palettes give each value of the sample variables the same color in every plot.

data(count_table)
data(annotation_table)

samples <- data.frame(
    Sample = c("Time1", "Time2",
        paste0("Time3_TRT_", c("A", "B", "C")),
        paste0("Time3_CTRL_", c("A", "B", "C")),
        paste0("Time4_TRT_", c("A", "B", "C")),
        paste0("Time4_CTRL_", c("A", "B", "C"))),
    Day = c("Time1", "Time2", rep(c("Time3", "Time4"), each = 6)),
    Treatment = c("Time1", "Time2", rep(rep(c("TRT", "CTRL"), each = 3), 2))
)
groups <- factor(ifelse(samples$Day %in% c("Time1", "Time2"), "T1/T2",
    paste(samples$Day, samples$Treatment, sep = "_")))

counts <- filter(count_table, Barcode != "*")
colnames(counts) <- c("Barcode", samples$Sample)

object <- create_screenr_object(
    table = counts, annotation = annotation_table, groups = groups,
    sample_table = samples,
    palettes = list(
        Treatment = c(Time1 = "#CCCCCC", Time2 = "#999999",
            CTRL = "#1B9E77", TRT = "#D95F02"),
        Day = c(Time1 = "#CCCCCC", Time2 = "#999999",
            Time3 = "#7570B3", Time4 = "#E7298A"),
        Group = c(`T1/T2` = "#999999", Time3_CTRL = "#66C2A5",
            Time3_TRT = "#FC8D62", Time4_CTRL = "#1B9E77",
            Time4_TRT = "#D95F02")
    )
)
object <- remove_all_zero_row(object)
get_sample_table(object)
#> # A tibble: 14 × 3
#>    Sample       Day   Treatment
#>    <chr>        <chr> <chr>    
#>  1 Time1        Time1 Time1    
#>  2 Time2        Time2 Time2    
#>  3 Time3_TRT_A  Time3 TRT      
#>  4 Time3_TRT_B  Time3 TRT      
#>  5 Time3_TRT_C  Time3 TRT      
#>  6 Time3_CTRL_A Time3 CTRL     
#>  7 Time3_CTRL_B Time3 CTRL     
#>  8 Time3_CTRL_C Time3 CTRL     
#>  9 Time4_TRT_A  Time4 TRT      
#> 10 Time4_TRT_B  Time4 TRT      
#> 11 Time4_TRT_C  Time4 TRT      
#> 12 Time4_CTRL_A Time4 CTRL     
#> 13 Time4_CTRL_B Time4 CTRL     
#> 14 Time4_CTRL_C Time4 CTRL

The counts are normalized once, and the same normalization is used by every function below: the hit-finding methods, the fold changes and the plots. TMM is used here, as in the longitudinal vignette (see ?normalize_data for the methods and for when TMM is biased).

object <- normalize_data(object, method = "tmm")
get_normalization(object)$method
#> [1] "tmm"

Overview of the methods

Method Function What it tests Reference Uses replicates
FRY find_roast_hit(method = "fry") The barcodes of the gene change None (self-contained) Yes
ROAST find_roast_hit() As FRY, with random rotations None (self-contained) Yes
CAMERA find_camera_hit() The barcodes of the gene change more than the others The other genes (competitive) Yes
Gene-level Z-score find_gene_zscore_hit() The mean Z-score of the barcodes of the gene is extreme Random sets of barcodes, or the empirical null With compute_barcode_statistics()
All time points find_consistent_hit() The gene changes at every time point As the chosen method Yes
Time course find_time_hit() The treatment effect changes over time None Yes
Legacy Z-score rules find_zscore_hit(), find_robust_zscore_hit() Counts barcodes below the median Z-score None No

The FDR (false discovery rate) is the expected proportion of false hits among the genes you call hits: with an FDR cut off of 5%, about 1 in 20 of the reported genes is expected to be a false positive. Each method returns only the genes with FDR <= fdr (default 0.05); use fdr = 1 to get all the genes and rank them yourself, as done below.

Step 1: which samples to compare

The methods that use the replicates fit a linear model, which needs two things:

  • a design matrix, which says which group each sample belongs to;
  • a contrast, which says which groups to compare.

create_design_matrix() builds the design matrix from the groups of the object: one column per group, and a 1 in the column of the group of each sample. Group names that are not valid R names are changed (T1/T2 becomes T1.T2).

design <- create_design_matrix(object)
design
#>              T1.T2 Time3_CTRL Time3_TRT Time4_CTRL Time4_TRT
#> Time1            1          0         0          0         0
#> Time2            1          0         0          0         0
#> Time3_TRT_A      0          0         1          0         0
#> Time3_TRT_B      0          0         1          0         0
#> Time3_TRT_C      0          0         1          0         0
#> Time3_CTRL_A     0          1         0          0         0
#> Time3_CTRL_B     0          1         0          0         0
#> Time3_CTRL_C     0          1         0          0         0
#> Time4_TRT_A      0          0         0          0         1
#> Time4_TRT_B      0          0         0          0         1
#> Time4_TRT_C      0          0         0          0         1
#> Time4_CTRL_A     0          0         0          1         0
#> Time4_CTRL_B     0          0         0          1         0
#> Time4_CTRL_C     0          0         0          1         0
#> attr(,"assign")
#> [1] 1 1 1 1 1
#> attr(,"contrasts")
#> attr(,"contrasts")$groups
#> [1] "contr.treatment"

create_contrast() builds the comparison between groups by name: here treated against control at each time point.

contrast_time3 <- create_contrast(design,
    treatment = "Time3_TRT", control = "Time3_CTRL"
)
contrast_time4 <- create_contrast(design,
    treatment = "Time4_TRT", control = "Time4_CTRL"
)
contrast_time4
#>      T1.T2 Time3_CTRL  Time3_TRT Time4_CTRL  Time4_TRT 
#>          0          0          0         -1          1

The contrast gives +1 to the treated group and -1 to the control group: the result is the treated minus the control. With several groups on one side (for example treatment = c("Time3_TRT", "Time4_TRT")) their average is used.

Common mistake. Do not build the design with model.matrix(~ groups) and rename its columns: the first group becomes the intercept and the columns are in alphabetical order, so the names end up on the wrong columns and the wrong samples are compared. create_design_matrix() and create_contrast() avoid this, and every function that takes a design checks that its rows are the samples of the object, in the same order.

The examples below compare treated and control samples at Time4, the time point with the larger effect.

Step 2: FRY, ROAST and CAMERA

These methods test the barcodes of each gene as a set, with edgeR on the raw counts and the normalization of the object.

  • FRY and ROAST ask whether the barcodes of a gene change at all (a self-contained test). ROAST uses random rotations: set seed to get the same result every time and use many rotations (nrot, default 9999) for a real analysis; here 999 keep the tutorial fast. FRY (method = "fry") computes the same test exactly, without rotations: it is faster, its p-values are not limited by the number of rotations, and it is the recommended choice.
  • CAMERA asks whether the barcodes of a gene change more than the other barcodes (a competitive test), taking into account the correlation between barcodes.

The two kinds of tests answer different questions. A self-contained test calls a gene when its barcodes are depleted more than the replicates vary, even if many genes are depleted; a competitive test calls it only when it stands out from the rest of the library, so it becomes conservative when many genes have an effect. On the other hand FRY and ROAST rely on the variability between replicates: they need replicates in both groups, have little power with two replicates or noisy data, and find almost nothing when the control is a single sample (for example a plasmid library). All the p-values are one-sided, for the requested direction.

number_barcode sets the minimum number of barcodes (more than number_barcode) a gene needs to be tested, and direction chooses depleted ("Down") or enriched ("Up") genes.

fry <- find_roast_hit(object, design, contrast_time4,
    method = "fry", fdr = 1
)
head(fry)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   Gene     NGenes Direction    PValue    FDR  PValue.Mixed  FDR.Mixed Log2FC
#>   <chr>     <int> <fct>         <dbl>  <dbl>         <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_173     10 Down      0.0000891 0.0191 0.00000244    0.000217   -0.500
#> 2 Gene_422     10 Down      0.0000933 0.0191 0.0000525     0.00156    -0.419
#> 3 Gene_412     10 Down      0.000107  0.0191 0.00000579    0.000309   -0.311
#> 4 Gene_15      10 Down      0.000166  0.0191 0.00724       0.0390     -0.310
#> 5 Gene_296     10 Down      0.000179  0.0191 0.0158        0.0615     -0.491
#> 6 Gene_349     10 Down      0.000365  0.0325 0.00000000678 0.00000121 -0.167

roast <- find_roast_hit(object, design, contrast_time4,
    nrot = 999, seed = 42, fdr = 1
)
camera <- find_camera_hit(object, design, contrast_time4, fdr = 1)
head(camera)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   Gene     NGenes Direction   PValue    FDR Log2FC
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <fct>        <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_173     10 Down      0.000218 0.0767 -0.500
#> 2 Gene_296     10 Down      0.000421 0.0767 -0.491
#> 3 Gene_422     10 Down      0.000431 0.0767 -0.419
#> 4 Gene_352     10 Down      0.00179  0.230  -0.455
#> 5 Gene_87      10 Down      0.00241  0.230  -0.422
#> 6 Gene_370     10 Down      0.00300  0.230  -0.330
Column Meaning
NGenes Number of barcodes of the gene
Direction Down or Up
PValue, FDR Significance for the requested direction
PValue.Mixed, FDR.Mixed (FRY, ROAST) Significance of a change in either direction of the barcodes
PropDown, PropUp (ROAST) Proportion of barcodes going down or up
Log2FC Median log2 fold change of the barcodes

Use PValue and FDR: the “Mixed” columns test whether the barcodes change in any direction, so they also call genes whose barcodes disagree.

Step 3: the Z-score methods

Fold changes and Z-scores

compute_metrics() averages the replicates of the treated and of the control samples of one time point and computes for each barcode:

Column Meaning
Treated, Control Mean normalized count
Log2FC log2((Treated + 0.5) / (Control + 0.5)): negative means depleted in the treated samples
Zscore Log2FC standardized with the mean and standard deviation of all barcodes
ZscoreRobust Log2FC standardized with the median and MAD, less sensitive to outliers

The treatment and control arguments are values of the Treatment column of get_sample_table(), and day a value of its Day column.

metrics_time3 <- compute_metrics(object,
    control = "CTRL", treatment = "TRT", day = "Time3"
)
metrics_time4 <- compute_metrics(object,
    control = "CTRL", treatment = "TRT", day = "Time4"
)
head(metrics_time4)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 9
#>   Barcode Gene     Treated Control Log2FC Zscore ZscoreRobust Day   Treatment
#>   <fct>   <chr>      <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>        <dbl> <chr> <chr>    
#> 1 10208   Gene_380   395.    365.   0.111  0.289        0.331 Time4 TRT      
#> 2 10502   Gene_380    27.8    37.9 -0.441 -0.863       -1.25  Time4 TRT      
#> 3 10796   Gene_380    35.7    59.0 -0.718 -1.44        -2.04  Time4 TRT      
#> 4 11089   Gene_380   294.    327.  -0.152 -0.259       -0.421 Time4 TRT      
#> 5 11382   Gene_380    26.8    43.0 -0.671 -1.34        -1.91  Time4 TRT      
#> 6 11675   Gene_380   813.    982.  -0.272 -0.509       -0.764 Time4 TRT

plot_zscore_distribution() compares the Z-scores of several time points: a treatment with an effect gives a longer left tail at the later time point. It receives the tables, not the object, so the palette of the time points is given explicitly to keep the colors of the other plots:

plot_zscore_distribution(
    list(Time3 = metrics_time3, Time4 = metrics_time4),
    alpha = 0.6, palette = get_palettes(object)$Day
)

Using the replicates

compute_metrics() averages the replicates, so it cannot tell a consistent barcode from a noisy one. compute_barcode_statistics() tests each barcode with edgeR, using the variability between replicates, and returns a Z-score with the same columns. This is the recommended input of the gene-level test.

barcode_statistics <- compute_barcode_statistics(
    object, design, contrast_time4
)
head(barcode_statistics)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   Barcode Gene     Log2FC logCPM     F PValue   FDR Zscore
#>   <chr>   <chr>     <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 10208   Gene_380  0.124   8.56 0.566 0.455  0.801  0.748
#> 2 10502   Gene_380 -0.464   4.97 0.702 0.405  0.776 -0.832
#> 3 10796   Gene_380 -0.650   6.60 2.36  0.129  0.525 -1.52 
#> 4 11089   Gene_380 -0.153   8.44 0.818 0.369  0.749 -0.898
#> 5 11382   Gene_380 -0.636   5.62 1.37  0.247  0.655 -1.16 
#> 6 11675   Gene_380 -0.271   9.66 5.92  0.0178 0.251 -2.37

Gene-level test

find_gene_zscore_hit() computes for each gene the mean Z-score of its barcodes (statistic = "median" uses the median, which is less affected by a single barcode with a strong, possibly off-target, effect) and compares it with a reference distribution:

  • reference = "random" (default): the scores of random sets of barcodes of the same size, drawn n_permutations times (seed makes it reproducible). With control_genes the random sets are drawn from control genes instead. Do this only if the controls behave like genes without effect: non-targeting shRNAs often do not (targeting shRNAs are usually somewhat depleted compared with them, so every gene looks depleted).
  • reference = "empirical": the distribution of the scores of the genes without effect, estimated from the centre of the distribution of all the genes. It accounts for the barcodes of a gene varying together, which makes the random sets give too small p-values, especially in shRNA screens. It needs a library with hundreds of genes, most of them without effect (see the empirical null vignette).
zscore <- find_gene_zscore_hit(barcode_statistics, fdr = 1, seed = 1)
zscore_empirical <- find_gene_zscore_hit(barcode_statistics,
    reference = "empirical", fdr = 1
)
head(zscore_empirical)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   Gene     NBarcodes Score Log2FC Statistic   PValue    FDR
#>   <chr>        <int> <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_173        10 -1.53 -0.506     -3.65 0.000135 0.0719
#> 2 Gene_422        10 -1.39 -0.436     -3.31 0.000474 0.127 
#> 3 Gene_15         10 -1.31 -0.305     -3.12 0.000901 0.155 
#> 4 Gene_296        10 -1.28 -0.477     -3.05 0.00116  0.155 
#> 5 Gene_370        10 -1.19 -0.378     -2.83 0.00235  0.223 
#> 6 Gene_168        10 -1.15 -0.242     -2.74 0.00306  0.223
Column Meaning
NBarcodes Number of barcodes of the gene
Score Mean Z-score of the barcodes
Log2FC Median log2 fold change of the barcodes
PValue, FDR Significance

plot_empirical_null() shows the gene scores and the fitted null, which should follow the centre of the distribution:

plot_empirical_null(barcode_statistics)

Here the null is almost the standard normal (mean 0.01, standard deviation 1), with no long tail of depleted genes: the treatment effect is moderate and concerns a few genes.

Legacy rules

find_zscore_hit() and find_robust_zscore_hit() call a gene a hit when more than number_barcode of its barcodes are below the median Z-score. They are kept for compatibility, but they do not give a p-value and many genes without an effect pass them by chance (about 17% with 10 barcodes and number_barcode = 6): prefer find_gene_zscore_hit().

nrow(find_zscore_hit(metrics_time4, number_barcode = 6))
#> [1] 96

Step 4: comparing and combining the methods

How many genes each method finds 

results <- list(
    FRY = fry, ROAST = roast, CAMERA = camera,
    `Z-score` = zscore, `Z-score (empirical)` = zscore_empirical
)
fdr_levels <- c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25)
bind_rows(lapply(results, function(result) {
    vapply(fdr_levels, function(x) sum(result$FDR <= x), integer(1))
}), .id = "Method") %>%
    mutate(FDR = paste0(100 * fdr_levels, "%"), .before = 1)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   FDR     FRY ROAST CAMERA `Z-score` `Z-score (empirical)`
#>   <chr> <int> <int>  <int>     <int>                 <int>
#> 1 5%        7     0      0         0                     0
#> 2 10%      12    10      3         0                     1
#> 3 25%      34    28      7         4                     8

FRY, the most powerful test here, finds 7 genes at 5% FDR. ROAST tests the same hypothesis, but with 999 rotations its p-values cannot be smaller than 1/1000, which after the correction for the 283 genes is not enough to reach 5% (use nrot = 9999, or FRY). The competitive tests (CAMERA and the Z-score tests) find none at 5%: the depletions are reproducible, but they do not stand out against all the other genes of the library. Choose the cut off before looking at the results and report it; below, 10% is used to compare the methods.

Overlap between the methods

plot_common_hit() takes the results of any number of methods (any table with Gene and FDR) and shows the overlap of their hits at the cut off given with fdr. With up to three methods it draws a Venn diagram:

plot_common_hit(results[c("FRY", "ROAST", "CAMERA")], fdr = 0.1,
    title = "Depleted genes at Time4 (10% FDR)")

With more methods it draws an UpSet plot: each column is a combination of methods (the dots below), and the bar on top counts the genes found by exactly that combination; the bars on the left count the genes found by each method.

plot_common_hit(results, fdr = 0.1,
    title = "Depleted genes at Time4 (10% FDR)")

find_common_hit() returns the genes found by at least common_in methods (by default by all of them):

common <- find_common_hit(results, fdr = 0.1, common_in = 3)
common
#> [1] "Gene_173" "Gene_422" "Gene_296"

summarise_hits() puts the FDR of every method in one table. NMethods counts the methods in which the gene passes the cut off, and MaxFDR (the largest FDR) is a conservative score to rank the genes supported by all the methods. Pass the tables computed with fdr = 1, so that every gene has a value.

summary <- summarise_hits(results, fdr = 0.1)
summary %>%
    select(Gene, starts_with("FDR"), NMethods) %>%
    head(8) %>%
    knitr::kable(digits = 3)
Gene FDR_FRY FDR_ROAST FDR_CAMERA FDR_Z-score FDR_Z-score (empirical) NMethods
Gene_173 0.019 0.076 0.077 0.123 0.072 4
Gene_422 0.019 0.076 0.077 0.192 0.127 3
Gene_296 0.019 0.076 0.077 0.203 0.155 3
Gene_15 0.019 0.076 0.230 0.203 0.155 2
Gene_370 0.132 0.144 0.230 0.271 0.223 0
Gene_352 0.185 0.173 0.230 0.271 0.223 0
Gene_87 0.261 0.267 0.230 0.271 0.223 0
Gene_349 0.032 0.076 0.254 0.363 0.311 2

plot_volcano() shows every gene with its effect (x) and its significance (y): the hits are above the dashed line, and the most significant are labelled. Here the 12 genes that FRY finds at 10% FDR:

plot_volcano(fry, fdr = 0.1)

With the table of summarise_hits() the significance is the largest FDR of the methods, so the genes above the line are found by every method; give the barcode statistics, from which the mean log2 fold change of each gene is computed: plot_volcano(summary, statistics = barcode_statistics). None of the genes of this screen is found by all five methods at 10% FDR.

The combined list has no guaranteed false discovery rate: treat it as a short list of candidates to check and validate.

Step 5: several time points

“Depleted over time” can mean different things, which need different tests.

Depleted at every time point

find_consistent_hit() runs the same method for several contrasts and calls a gene only if it is depleted in all of them (an intersection-union test: the p-value of the gene is the largest of its p-values, then corrected for the number of genes).

consistent <- find_consistent_hit(object, design,
    contrasts = list(Time3 = contrast_time3, Time4 = contrast_time4),
    method = "fry", fdr = 1
)
head(consistent)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 9
#>   Gene     Direction NContrasts  PValue   FDR PValue_Time3 Log2FC_Time3
#>   <chr>    <chr>          <int>   <dbl> <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_173 Down               2 0.00986 1.000      0.00986      -0.211 
#> 2 Gene_457 Down               2 0.0377  1.000      0.00858      -0.121 
#> 3 Gene_121 Down               2 0.0428  1.000      0.0428       -0.0741
#> 4 Gene_293 Down               2 0.0516  1.000      0.0516       -0.134 
#> 5 Gene_394 Down               2 0.0577  1.000      0.0577       -0.0813
#> 6 Gene_377 Down               2 0.0707  1.000      0.00138      -0.249 
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: PValue_Time4 <dbl>, Log2FC_Time4 <dbl>

The smallest FDR is 1: no gene is depleted at both time points. The candidates of Time4 have small effects at Time3 (see Log2FC_Time3), so in this screen the treatment-specific depletion appears at the later time point. combine_consistent_hits() does the same with tables of p-values computed beforehand.

A treatment effect that changes over time

find_time_hit() asks whether the treatment effect changes over time, with one model for the treated and control samples of all the time points: untreated and treated samples each follow a line over time, and the method tests the difference between the slopes. Give the real times of the time points with time (here days after the selection); otherwise they are treated as equally spaced. Samples taken before the treatment can be added as untreated samples with baseline, when their times are known too.

time_hit <- find_time_hit(object,
    treatment = "TRT", control = "CTRL",
    days = c("Time3", "Time4"), time = c(Time3 = 7, Time4 = 14),
    fdr = 1
)
head(time_hit)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   Gene     NGenes Direction   PValue   FDR  Log2FC
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <fct>        <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_296     10 Down      0.000596 0.318 -0.0964
#> 2 Gene_372     12 Down      0.00156  0.323 -0.104 
#> 3 Gene_422     10 Down      0.00181  0.323 -0.0672
#> 4 Gene_412     10 Down      0.00480  0.483 -0.0812
#> 5 Gene_419     10 Down      0.00510  0.483 -0.0826
#> 6 Gene_87      10 Down      0.00566  0.483 -0.0585

Log2FC is the change of the treatment log2 fold change per day: a negative value means that the depletion grows over time. With two time points this is the difference between the effects at Time4 and at Time3, divided by 7 days. Here 0 genes have an FDR below 5% (smallest FDR 0.32): the effects grow between the two time points, but not enough to be detected gene by gene with three replicates.

Step 6: checking the candidates

Statistics can produce false positives, so look at the data of each candidate. The candidates here are the genes found by at least three of the five methods at 10% FDR:

candidates <- common
candidates
#> [1] "Gene_173" "Gene_422" "Gene_296"

Trend over time

plot_trend() shows the mean normalized count of the barcodes of a gene in each sample over the time points. With color_by the treated and control samples get their own trend (the mean of each time point), the samples before the treatment are drawn once as shared references (reference_groups), and highlight_difference shades the gap between the two conditions. A treatment-specific hit goes down in the treated samples more than in the controls.

plot_trend(object,
    genes = candidates, group_var = c("Time1", "Time2", "CTRL", "TRT"),
    color_by = "Treatment", reference_groups = c("Time1", "Time2"),
    connect_reference = TRUE, highlight_difference = TRUE,
    nrow = 1, scales = "free_y"
) +
    labs(x = "Time point (equally spaced)",
        y = "Mean normalized counts per shRNA")

Size of the effect

plot_treatment_separation() shows the log2 ratio of the treated to the control samples at each time point, labelled with the percentage difference. It shows how far the conditions separate and at which time point; it is descriptive, not a test.

Gene_173 and Gene_422 decrease in the treated samples while the controls stay stable or grow. Gene_296 decreases in the controls too (its knockdown slows growth even without the treatment), and more in the treated samples: the treatment adds to a fitness effect.

plot_treatment_separation(object, candidates,
    treatment = "TRT", control = "CTRL", nrow = 1
)

Distribution of the barcodes

plot_boxplot() shows the normalized counts of all the barcodes of a gene in each sample, colored by the variable given with fill_var (here with the palette of the Treatment):

plot_boxplot(object,
    genes = candidates[1], group_var = c("TRT", "CTRL"),
    fill_var = "Treatment"
) +
    scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 45))

Barcode by barcode

A real hit should be supported by most of its barcodes, not by one or two. plot_barcode_heatmap() shows every barcode of the genes in every sample, centred on the mean of the barcode across the samples shown: blue is lower and red higher than the usual abundance of the barcode.

plot_barcode_heatmap(object, candidates, column_group = "Day") +
    scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 60))

At Time4 several barcodes of each gene are lower in the treated samples than in the controls, so the depletion is not driven by a single barcode; it is clearest for Gene_296. The effects are moderate, and they vary between the replicates.

plot_barcode_trend() shows the log2 fold change of each barcode at each time point (it returns one plot per gene):

barcode_trends <- plot_barcode_trend(
    list(Time3 = metrics_time3, Time4 = metrics_time4),
    genes = candidates[1]
)
barcode_trends[[candidates[1]]]

plot_barcode_hit() ranks all the barcodes by their log2 fold change and places the barcodes of a gene on the ranking (vertical lines): most lines on the left side means that the gene is depleted. The line on top shows where the barcodes of the gene are concentrated (above 1, dashed line), and the bottom panel shows their log2 fold changes (show_log2fc = FALSE hides it):

plot_barcode_hit(object, design,
    contrast = contrast_time4, gene = candidates[1]
)

find_discordant_barcodes() lists the barcodes that behave very differently from the other barcodes of their gene, which may have off-target effects. They are a warning to read the result of the gene with care; do not remove them before the tests.

discordant <- find_discordant_barcodes(metrics_time4, threshold = 3)
filter(discordant, Gene %in% candidates)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 5
#> # ℹ 5 variables: Barcode <fct>, Gene <chr>, Log2FC <dbl>, GeneLog2FC <dbl>,
#> #   Deviation <dbl>

Additional filters

Two filters can remove candidates that are not convincing:

  • filter_by_slope() keeps the genes whose normalized counts decrease more over time in the treated samples than in the control samples (with time, the slopes are per unit of time);
  • filter_by_variance() removes the genes whose barcodes disagree too much (variance of the barcode log2 fold changes above variance).
filter_by_slope(object,
    genes = candidates,
    group_var_treatment = "TRT", group_var_control = "CTRL",
    time = c(Time3 = 7, Time4 = 14)
)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   Gene     slope_control slope_treatment
#>   <chr>            <dbl>           <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_173          1.14          -3.47 
#> 2 Gene_296         -4.64          -8.92 
#> 3 Gene_422          2.98          -0.680

filter_by_variance(object,
    genes = candidates, matrix_model = design,
    contrast = contrast_time4, variance = 0.5
) %>%
    distinct(Gene, Variance)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   Gene     Variance
#>   <chr>       <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_173    0.325
#> 2 Gene_296    0.287
#> 3 Gene_422    0.226

Summary

Step What to do
1 create_design_matrix() and create_contrast() for the comparison
2 find_roast_hit(method = "fry"); find_camera_hit() for a competitive test
3 compute_barcode_statistics() + find_gene_zscore_hit(), with reference = "empirical" for shRNA libraries
4 plot_common_hit(), find_common_hit(), summarise_hits() and plot_volcano()
5 find_consistent_hit() (every time point) and find_time_hit() (an effect that changes over time)
6 plot_trend(), plot_treatment_separation(), plot_boxplot(), plot_barcode_heatmap(), plot_barcode_hit(), find_discordant_barcodes()

Choose the FDR cut off before the analysis, report it, and validate the candidates experimentally. The longitudinal screen vignette puts these steps together and ends with the genes of this screen to validate.
